comment.value: This work presents EyeGraph, a new dataset for eye-tracking based on event camera. Three reviewers reviewed this work, and addressed certain concerns such as limitations of single-eye tracking, eye-tracking ground-truth, experimental settings, comparisons with more SOTA. By rebuttals and replies exchanged between the authors and reviewers, the authors clarified the issues, and the reviewers showed their support with the hope that the issues addressed will be addressed in the final version of this work.

We are pleased to see the reviewer's positive acknowledgement of our rebuttal and their upgraded score on our paper. Once again, we are grateful to the reviewer for their constructive feedback on our work, which has helped to further improve the quality of our manuscript.

We acknowledge and thank all the anonymous reviewers for the actionable and constructive feedback provided. We have carefully considered their suggestions and critiques and will respond to them individually in the following sections.

In summary, we address the following comments and attach a one-page revision document that depicts some of our recent results:
1. Limitations of monocular eye tracking [WpCY, F7PD]
2. Lack of in-the-wild settings in the experimental setup [WpCY, F7PD, 6Wc6]
3. Eye-tracking ground-truth [F7PD, 6Wc6]
4. The impact of head movement and eye rotation degrees [WpCY]
5. Comparisons with more recent state-of-the-art methods including supervised techniques [F7PD, 6Wc6]
6. Future work and potential applications of EyeGraph dataset and the proposed unsupervised graph-based approach [F7PD]

In our one-page pdf, we add the following results/plots:
1.  t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) of 10 selected subjects from the Ev-Eye dataset [13] and show that different subjects have distinctive, non-overlapping distributions of the features, strongly suggesting that these monocular features can be used to authenticate individual subjects.
2.  The distribution of (temporally) consecutive events in the event data sample of a randomly selected participant to show the actual temporal resolution propagated through our pipeline
3. Performance of proposed unsupervised pipeline for pupil coordinates estimation compared against the most competitive clustering baseline across 3ET+ measured by p-score evaluation metrics and error distances
4. Performance of proposed unsupervised pipeline for pupil coordinates estimation compared against the most recent supervised SOTA across our dataset with respect to p-score evaluation metrics and error distances

Please let us know if any of our responses are unclear or if a new question or comment comes up. We will do our best to clarify any ambiguities and further comments.

We appreciate the reviewer’s careful review of our manuscript, their time and insightful suggestions.

**[6Wc6-C1] Temporal resolution:** As the reviewer pointed out, event cameras record asynchronous events with a sub-microsecond latency. It is noteworthy to highlight that, unlike other frame-based event representations used in previous works [14, 13], our (dynamic) graph-based event representation fully preserves the entire temporal resolution delivered by the event camera and propagates through the rest of the pipeline. Further, the rest of our method including EyeGraph graph clustering and tube-based RANSAC model does not overlook or reduce the temporal resolution preserved by event graphs but rather propagates that resolution until the final downstream task: pupil coordinates estimation. Therefore, it is possible for EyeGraph to continuously predict the pupil coordinates with the fullest temporal resolution delivered by the event camera stream and is only restricted by the hardware limitations of the utilized event camera i.e., DAVIS346 (https://inivation.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/2021-08-iniVation-devices-Specifications.pdf) in which the achievable temporal resolution is $1 \mu s$. To further extend our analysis, we plot the distribution of (temporally) consecutive events in event data of a randomly selected subject in our one-page PDF revision to show the actual temporal resolution propagated through our pipeline. The average time between two consecutive events is approximately 8 micro-seconds with a nominal event frequency of 125,000 Hz in the representative example.

**[6Wc6-C2] Lack of in-the-wild settings in the dataset:** We acknowledge that our current version of the manuscript does not adequately capture the diversity of in-the-wild settings, especially in terms of continuous fluctuation of ambient lighting conditions.  We shall reposition our current claim as follows: *EyeGraph dataset is collected under several representative real-world lighting conditions, such as outdoor, standard-lit room, dimly-lit room and luminance interchanging under two lit-states*. Furthermore, we collect new instances while retaining the replicable visual stimulus under more naturalistic in-the-wild settings, characterized by possible continuous variation in ambient luminance (separately measured near the eye with a LUX monitor) while performing diverse activities such as walking. 

**[6Wc6-C3] Benchmarking other clustering methods:** As we report in Table 3 in the paper, DMoN [15] is the most competitive clustering baseline, and thus in this rebuttal, we evaluate the performance of DMoN by replacing only EyeGraph clustering method in our pipeline i.e, the rest of the pipeline including dynamic graph construction, cluster selection, and RANSAC-based coordinates estimation remained unchanged. Please note that we exactly follow the steps we have taken to build k-means-based supervised implementation (i.e., k-means-1) here, as described in Section 5.3 in supplementary materials. The results are shown in the table below. We can see that the incorporation of the EyeGraph clustering approach is beneficial even to the DMoN approach, as it helps achieve $\approx$ 14\% improvement in the p\_10 values.


**Table:** Performance of our pipeline for pupil estimation across 3ET+. *Only clustering method is replaced in our pipeline.

| Category     | Method       | p10$\uparrow$  | p5$\uparrow$   | p1$\uparrow$   | $l_2$ $\downarrow$ | $l_1$ $\downarrow$ |
|--------------|--------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Unsupervised | DMoN (Ours)* | 77.45 | 75.07 | 10.20 | 8.36 | 9.66               |
|  Unsupervised | Ours         | 91.45 | 89.22 | 28.34 | 3.88 | 4.24 |


**[6Wc6-C4] Details on ground truth data:** Thank you! We addressed this comment in our response ``[WpCY-C2]``

**[6Wc6-C5] Minor comments on citation errors etc.:** We thank you for pointing these out. In the revised manuscript, we will carefully address these changes, as suggested.

**[6Wc6-C6] Discussion on the results:** We thank the reviewer for their suggestion. We will take appropriate measures to improve the clarity and readability of the results section.

**[6Wc6-C7] Compare with supervised methods:** We agree with the reviewer's comment. In this rebuttal, we have trained and evaluated one of the best-performing SOTA methods and reported the performance below. While the results from the SOTA method MambaPupil achieves slightly better performance (2\% improvement in p\_10 values) (as expected), we would like to highlight that our approach does not require any extensive training and labeling effort to achieve comparable performance (93\% vs 95\%).


**Table:** Performance of our pipeline for pupil coordinates estimation across our dataset

| Category     | Method                                 | p10$\uparrow$ | p5$\uparrow$ | p1$\uparrow$ | $l_2$ $\downarrow$ | $l_1$ $\downarrow$ |
|--------------|----------------------------------------|---------------|--------------|--------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Supervised   | MambaPupil | 95.88         | 87.04        | 40.77        | 3.11               | 3.33               |
| Unsupervised | Ours | 93.67         | 91.78        | 31.90        | 3.54               | 3.98               |

**[6Wc6-C8] Present experiment results for each condition separately:** We are grateful for the reviewer's valuable suggestion. We extend Section 5 of the supplementary materials, named ``Supplements for Experiments and Results``, by including condition-wise (i.e., for each experimental setup) results.


13. G. Zhao, et al. Ev-eye: Rethinking high-frequency eye tracking through the lenses of event cameras. NeurIPS, 2024
14. Z. Wang et al. Mambapupil: Bidirectional selective recurrent model for event-based eye tracking. CVPR, 2024b.
15. A. Tsitsulin et al. Graph clustering with graph neural networks. JMLR, 24(127), 2023.

We truly appreciate the reviewer’s thorough evaluation of our manuscript and their constructive feedback.

**[F7PD-C1] Limitations of single-eye tracking:** Thank you for pointing out this feedback. Please see our response in ``[WpCY-C1]``, where we have addressed this commonly-expressed feedback.

**[F7PD-C2] Inclusion of natural stimuli and real-world interaction scenarios:** We acknowledge the merits of the reviewer's suggestion to include more natural cue-based stimuli, via real-world interaction scenarios, in future data collection efforts. We are already working to address this partially within the timeframe of our current submission: as we mention in the datasheet for dataset (section 6.7 in supplementary materials), we are working to augment our dataset, and/or release new iterations,  with more naturalistic, but visual stimuli-driven, in-the-wild studies in both indoor and outdoor environments so as to capture finer-grained continuous variation in illuminance, and during diverse set of physical activities. We provided a detailed response in ``[WpCY-C4]``

**[F7PD-C3] Additional comparisons with more recent state-of-the-art methods:** We agree with the reviewer's concern about positioning the proposed benchmark with respect to the latest SOTA methods. To the best of our knowledge, we have compared and evaluated each novel contribution of our method: dynamic graph construction, EyeGraph graph clustering, and event-based pupil tracking, against the corresponding most recent and relevant SOTA methods including, but not limited to, [16, 17, 18, 19]. For example, in response ``[6Wc6-C7]`` we provide additional results in which we evaluated the *best* supervised event-based eye tracking algorithm and show that our EyeGraph approach achieves very comparable p\_10 values (with only 2\% lower).

**[F7PD-C4] Exploring the use of binocular eye-tracking:** While the studies have shown the velocity profiles between the two human eyes are similar (with very minimal and rare distinctions), we acknowledge that having binocular eye tracking data is more crucial specifically for medical diagnostics, while monocular tracking can be used where depth is not critical, such as user authentication, human-computer interaction etc. In our revised manuscript, we will expand the ``Limitations`` section of our paper to address the limitations of monocular eye tracking. Further, in response ``[WpCY-C1]``, we elaborate in detail about the limitations of monocular eye tracking and how binocular tracking can be beneficial in more crucial applications like physiological medical diagnostics.

**[F7PD-C5] Future work on potential applications:** We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. As mentioned earlier, we are already working on using this dataset to study the possible use of fine-grained pupillary movement for continuous biometric authentication. To guide the readership of the paper, we will extend the section 8: ``Discussion and Conclusion``, in the paper by including a new subsection on the potential future applications that could benefit (e.g., emotion recognition, cognitive load tracking) from both our methods and dataset.  Further, we look forward to applying our methods in other domains such as automotive vision and robotics.

**References:**

17. Z. Wang et al. Mambapupil: Bidirectional selective recurrent model for event-based eye tracking. IEEE/CVF CVPR, 2024b.

**[WpCY-C4] Lighting Conditions:** We acknowledge that our experimental setup does not adequately capture all the possible in-the-wild settings and a resulting time-series of variation in illuminance. Instead, it provides a discrete, but representative, set of combinations such as office setting (i.e., seated under standard illuminance), and dimmed illuminance (achieved by intermittently flickering the light switches). We are currently working to collect new instances under varying ambient conditions to update and release new iterations of the dataset. More specifically, we consider the continuous variation in the illuminance scenario (as the reviewer suggested) and conduct new experiments: the participant is now allowed to roam around freely (while carrying the laptop that shows the same visual stimuli we used earlier) both indoor and outdoor settings. Further, the walking trail includes physical locations that affect the illuminance, such as shaded trees, moving between two rooms with different lighting conditions, etc. We are responding to the reviewer feedback by collecting both the eye movement data, and close-to-eye illuminance readings using an additional LUX sensor, while an individual subject walks about both indoors and outdoors, over a range of conditions (e.g., early morning, afternoon, night). Our design choice of tracking only a single eye, which ensures that the individual's FoV remains completely unobstructed in one eye, becomes especially salient to prevent risks when exhibiting such natural movements in uncontrolled environments.

**[WpCY-C5] Negative Social Impact:** We thank the reviewer for the suggestion to specifically address the broader impacts of the work. We acknowledge that such eye-tracking based techniques may generate (a) inclusivity concerns, especially for individuals with sight impairments, and (b) privacy concerns, especially if emotions and cognitive stresses can be continually captured in workplaces.
We will update (a) the revised manuscript Section 4, and (b) the datasheet for datasets (section 6.2 in supplementary materials) accordingly. Further, we will add a separate subsection in supplementary materials (in Section 2: EyeGraph Dataset Details) where we thoroughly discuss the potential privacy considerations and our plan/instructions for the gated release of the dataset and codes.

**[WpCY-C2] Ground truth data:** The reviewer's understanding of the data collection mechanism is correct: the participants of our experimental study wore event-camera (head-mounted) and the off-the-shelf Pupil-Core tracker at separate stages (i.e., not simultaneously) during the collection process. We have collected Pupil-Core tracking data as a ``reference`` for cross-modal investigations (i.e., by replaying an identical visual stimulus across the two stages) rather than as ground truth. We believe that this approach is reasonable as our benchmark method is an ``event-only unsupervised`` eye tracking approach which does not need to depend on either (i) concurrent RGB frames as existing datasets [14, 13] or (ii) ground truth labels utilized in supervised approaches [15, 16, 17]. However, as reported in the paper (Section 7.4), we provide human-labelled ground truth pupil coordinates for event data collected during the following experimental setups: (1) changing ambient illuminance and (2) user mobility. In our ground truth generation process, we follow an event volume-based annotation procedure for labeling: both Python-based annotation code and the human-labeled ground truths are accessible through the link provided in the supplementary materials. We utilize these human-labelled ground truths to compare the performance of our method using our dataset against the existing supervised methods and clustering approaches. Further, for researchers who are interested in utilizing only Pupil-Core data for RGB-based gaze estimation or a related task, our EyeGraph dataset provides a rich collection of data (including raw near-eye videos, point of gaze and pupil coordinates, pupil/iris segmentation maps, annotations for fixations/blinks, world-view lookup etc.) -- prior to the data collection, the positions and angles of the three embedded cameras on the sliding arms of the tracker are mechanically adjusted. The tracker is calibrated using a 3D eye model-based calibration paradigm to mitigate the effects of potential head movement drifts.

**[WpCY-C3] Eye rotation degree:** We agree with the reviewer that the participants' gaze movements are influenced by the effect of head movements (i.e., the relationship between eye position and gaze direction is not static but rather dynamic, depending on the head's orientation relative to the stimuli [18]. This relationship has not proven to be material in existing datasets [15, 16, 17] since these were collected using fixed-head setups while restricting the natural head movements. However, to the best of our knowledge, it is not physiologically feasible to track stimuli using only head movements due to the vestibulo-ocular reflex. This reflex involuntarily stabilizes the human visual field and retinal image during head movements by inducing compensatory eye movements in the opposite direction, making it impractical to isolate head movement alone for tracking purposes [19]. Therefore, even under unrestricted head movement settings as in EyeGraph dataset collection,  eye movements remain the primary mechanism for visual exploration. Head movements serve a complementary role, extending or adjusting the visual range, but they naturally coordinate with eye movements, often following or aligning with them to track stimuli effectively. This tandem coordination ensures efficient and seamless visual tracking [18, 20].

We observe these coordinated eye and head movements in our dataset as well, specifically through the dense pupil coordinates, gaze angle, and velocity distribution with varying fields of view (as reported and empirically illustrated in our supplementary materials) given that the participants' head movements are unrestricted and natural. For researchers interested in incorporating head movement data into their analysis, our EyeGraph event data provides both inertial sensor measurements and external trigger data from the event camera. In addition, our EyeGraph Pupil-Core data has been collected by accounting head movements through a robust 3D eye-model-based calibration process. This process involved (1) adjusting the positions and angles of the three embedded cameras on the sliding arms of the Pupil-Core eye tracker to ensure optimal views, and (2) calibrating and validating the Pupil-Core eye tracker using a 5-point calibration paradigm, ensuring that the average calibration error remained below 1.5°, as measured by the Pupil Labs software. By following the reviewer's comments, we will update our supplementary materials by including the empirical illustrations of 3D pupil rotation angles and inertial measurements to further extend our analysis. To this end, we plot the temporal variations of the accelerometer and gyroscope using the inertial sensor measurements and the temporal variations of pupil rotation angles of a randomly selected sample (with the head movement) in our one-page PDF revision as exemplar illustrations.

**References:**

14.	A. N. Angelopoulos et al. Event-based near-eye gaze tracking beyond 10,000 hz. IEEE TVCG, 27(5): 2021.
15.	Q. Chen et al. 3et: Efficient event-based eye tracking using a change-based convlstm network. In 2023 IEEE BioCAS, 2023.
16.	Z. Wang et al. Event-based eye tracking. ais 2024 challenge survey. IEEE/CVF CVPR, 2024a. 
17.	Z. Wang et al. Mambapupil: Bidirectional selective recurrent model for event-based eye tracking. IEEE/CVF CVPR, 2024b.
18.	E. G. Freedman. Coordination of the eyes and head during visual orienting. Experimental brain research, 190, 2008.
19.	M. Fetter. Vestibulo-ocular reflex. Neuro-Ophthalmology, 40:35–51, 2007
20.	M. F. Land. Eye movements and the control of actions in everyday life. Progress in retinal and eye research, 25(3), 2006.

We thank the reviewer for taking the time to assess our manuscript and offering valuable suggestions.

**[WpCY-C1] Monocular Eye Tracking:** This is a common feedback, shared by multiple reviewers. As mentioned, our dataset only captures single pupillary movements for the following reasons:

1. In our approach, we focus on tracking the pupil's spatial coordinates rather than the trajectory of the gaze direction: pupil trajectory refers to the movement of the pupil within the eye over time, while the gaze direction represents the direction in which a person is looking relative to their environment. While correlated, pupil trajectory and gaze direction represent different aspects of eye movement. For example, changes in lighting conditions or cognitive load can cause fluctuations in pupil movement without necessarily corresponding to changes in gaze direction. Similarly, reflexive eye movements, such as saccades or smooth pursuit, can cause rapid changes in gaze direction while the pupil trajectory remains relatively stable.

2. Since we aim to track the reflexive, physiologically-driven spatiotemporal dynamics of the pupil (instead of gaze which requires depth information), we require only a single near-eye event camera. Our approach of tracking a single pupil is based on the assumption that users demonstrate ideal conjugate eye movements, reflecting synchronized ocular motions consistent with typical oculomotor function. Such single-pupil tracking also allows us to reduce the computational complexity of the event-processing pipeline.

3. Further, the broader understanding of saccadic and smooth pursuit eye movements suggests that both eyes move in a highly coordinated manner due to their control by shared neural circuits. Several works in vision science and ophthalmology discuss the stability and coordination of saccadic eye movements and imply that both eyes generally maintain similar velocity profiles, with the role of dominance not significantly altering this aspect of eye movement [1, 2, 3]

4. In addition, several prior works have used monocular eye tracking for: (a) 3D gaze tracking [4, 5], (b) emotion recognition [6, 7], (c) cognitive modelling [8, 9, 10], (d) virtual and mixed reality [11], and (e) user authentication [12].

5. Finally, the near-eye mounting of our event camera implies that our currently designed wearable results in partial obstruction of the field of view. Replicating this camera positioning of both eyes would have significantly obstructed an individual's vision, raising safety concerns and likely thwarting IRB approval. As mentioned above, single-eye tracking is seen to suffice for many non-medical use cases, and we thus believe that our dataset will provide benefits to such use cases and applications.

**Limitations:** While the studies have shown that the velocity profiles between the two human eyes are similar (with very minimal and rare distinctions), we recognize the critical importance of binocular eye tracking data to support physiological conditions/medical diagnostics use cases, such as capturing neurodevelopmental disorders. Conversely, monocular tracking proves to be sufficiently effective in applications where depth perception is not a priority, such as user authentication, human-computer interaction, and emotion recognition. To showcase the efficacy of single eye-tracking, in one of our ongoing unpublished research, we have been studying how the reflexive pupillary kinematics features vary across individuals (due to variations in ocular muscle strength), and can thus serve as a biometric fingerprint. In our one-page revision pdf, we plot the t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) of 10 selected subjects from the Ev-Eye dataset [13] and show that different subjects have distinctive, non-overlapping distributions of the features, strongly suggesting that these monocular features can be used to authenticate individual subjects.

In the revised manuscript, in Section 3, we will add a new subsection titled ``3.1 Monocular Eye Tracking`` and describe our rationale behind our choice of monocular eye tracking and the potential application that can benefit using single-eye-based eye movement features. Further, in Section 8, we will further extend the subsection ``Limitations`` and describe the limitations of monocular eye tracking.


**References:**
1. A. P. Morris, et al. Parietal stimulation destabilizes spatial updating across saccadic eye movements. PNAS, 2007
2. A. C. Schutz, et al. Eye movements and perception: A selective review. Journal of vision, 11(5):9–9, 2011.
3. R. J. Leigh et al. The neurology of eye movements. Oxford University Press, USA, 2015.
4. W. Zhu et al. Monocular free-head 3d gaze tracking with deep learning and geometry constraints. ICCV 2017.
5. M. Mansouryar et al. 3d gaze estimation from 2d pupil positions on monocular head-mounted eye trackers. ETRA, 2016.
6. H. Zhang et al. In the blink of an eye: Event-based emotion recognition. ACM SIGGRAPH, 2023.
7. H. Wu et al. Emo: Real-time emotion recognition from single-eye images for resource-constrained eyewear devices. MobiSys, 2020.
8. Y. Lim et al. Experimental characterisation of eye-tracking sensors for adaptive human-machine systems. Measurement, 140, 2019.
9. J. Johansson et al. Monocular and binocular reading performance in subjects with normal binocular vision. Clinical and Experimental Optometry, 97(4): 2014.
10. T. Heinen et al. Monocular and binocular vision in the performance of a complex skill. Journal of sports science & medicine, 10(3):520, 2011
11. I. Schuetz et al. Eye tracking in virtual reality: Vive pro eye spatial accuracy, precision, and calibration reliability. Journal of Eye Movement Research, 15(3), 2022.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper present a new dataset for eye-tracking based on event camera. The baseline use an unsupervised model to showcase the advantage of the dataset and algorithm.

review.value:
+ Event camera based eye-tracking dataset.
+ Large number of participant and various environment.

- Unclear about eye-tracking ground truth.
- Limited to one eye only.

The overall quality is good and clear to follow. The event camera based eye-tracking dataset has a broader audience for different applications. However, the dataset only contains 1 eye movement. The reason for only 1 eye was captured instead of both eyes are not clear, as wearable generally does not limit the capture of both eyes. While the event camera dataset can be used for eye feature extraction, it's not clear how the eye-tracking ground truth can be used for gaze estimation. From Figure 2, it seems the ground truth Pupil-core and event camera are not wear at the same time. Also, the eye rotation degrees are not clear in the dataset, especially when the head can move so potentially the participant can move head only to track the stimuli.

strengths.value: Event camera based eye-tracking dataset can be very interesting for other researchers. The proposed graph based method can be used as baseline to improve the performance on eye-tracking with event camera.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: A more clear ground truth. Also the lighting situation can be more diverse, such as multiple brightness and/or constant changing brightness. Using event camera to capture both eye for more practical application.

It introduces the EyeGraph dataset, which provides a large-scale, multi-modal near-eye tracking dataset. The proposed method addresses limitations of existing approaches by enhancing the tracking of pupillary movement using dynamic graph-based techniques. Contributions include the new dataset, innovative graph construction and clustering methods, and extensive experimental validation.

review.value: The paper introduces significant advancements in event-based eye-tracking by leveraging neuromorphic event cameras and dynamic graph-based methods. The EyeGraph dataset is a valuable contribution, offering rich and diverse features compared to traditional datasets. The proposed methods for dynamic graph construction and unsupervised clustering are well-motivated and demonstrated to outperform existing techniques. The experimental results are comprehensive and validate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach under various conditions.

summary_and_contributions.value:
The paper presents a novel approach to eye tracking using event-based cameras that capture changes asynchronously. It introduces "EyeGraph," a multi-modal near-eye tracking dataset collected with a wearable event camera attached to a head-mounted device. The authors propose a dynamic graph-based approach for high-fidelity tracking of pupillary movement using the event stream. The main contributions are:
1.	The introduction of the event-based eye-tracking dataset, EyeGraph, with varying ambient lighting and user mobility.
2.	An unsupervised topology-aware spatio-temporal graph clustering approach.
3.	Benchmarking against existing supervised SOTA algorithms and other baselines.

review.value:
Quality: The quality of the work is good. Data is collected with an event-based camera, and an unsupervised pipeline is proposed. 

Clarity: The written quality of the paper is good but could be improved.  

Originality: The pipeline is original but utilizes existing frameworks.  
Significance:  Good, this paper introduces an unsupervised framework for event-based eye tracking.

•	The event-based cameras record events with high temporal resolution asynchronously. However, the exact achieved temporal resolution is unclear.
•	The claim that the EyeGraph dataset mimics in-the-wild settings is not strongly supported by the described experimental setup, which remains relatively controlled with fixed luminance in the experimental conditions.
•	In Table 3, some other methods show better performance on SC, DB, and Cd metrics. Other clustering methods can be benchmarked in the entire pipeline to evaluate overall performance for pupil coordinates.
•	Details on ground truth data and its usage are missing.
•	The same paper is cited twice from two different sources [2,3]: Event-based near-eye gaze tracking beyond 10,000 Hz.
•	Line 22-23: The authors can add references for the application areas.
•	Line 101: References are missing.
•	Line 173: It would be helpful to indicate that {v_i, v_j} corresponds to the edge for clarity. For directed graphs, using the “(v_i, v_j)” notation would be clearer.
•	Line 203: P should be in a sentence with its description (P=...).

strengths.value:
•	The paper introduces a novel dynamic graph-based method for event-based eye tracking, addressing label sparsity, dense 2D framed representation, and RGB-based inference.
•	The EyeGraph dataset is a valuable contribution, providing data with different luminance levels and user movement.
•	The unsupervised clustering approach shows promising results, comparable to supervised methods.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
•	Clear discussion in the results section.
•	Applying supervised algorithms to the collected dataset would help highlight the differences in the dataset. Presenting experiment results for each condition separately would provide a better overview.
•	Other explanations and reference issues are already discussed in the reviews.

title.value: EyeGraph: Modularity-aware Spatio Temporal Graph Clustering for Continuous Event-based Eye Tracking

TLDR.value: Our paper presents EyeGraph, a large-scale multi-modal near-eye tracking dataset curated while mimicking in-the-wild settings, and an unsupervised modularity-aware graph clustering technique for continuous eye tracking.

abstract.value: Continuous tracking of eye movement dynamics plays a significant role in developing a broad spectrum of human-centered applications, such as cognitive skills (visual attention and working memory) modeling, human-machine interaction, biometric user authentication, and foveated rendering. Recently neuromorphic cameras have garnered significant interest in the eye-tracking research community, owing to their sub-microsecond latency in capturing intensity changes resulting from eye movements. Nevertheless, the existing approaches for event-based eye tracking suffer from several limitations: dependence on RGB frames, label sparsity, and training on datasets collected in controlled lab environments that do not adequately reflect real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, in this paper, we propose a dynamic graph-based approach that uses a neuromorphic event stream captured by Dynamic Vision Sensors (DVS) for high-fidelity tracking of pupillary movement. More specifically, first, we present EyeGraph, a large-scale multi-modal near-eye tracking dataset collected using a wearable event camera attached to a head-mounted device from 40 participants -- the dataset was curated while mimicking in-the-wild settings, accounting for varying mobility and ambient lighting conditions. Subsequently, to address the issue of label sparsity, we adopt an unsupervised topology-aware approach as a benchmark. To be specific, (a) we first construct a dynamic graph using Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM), resulting in a uniform and detailed representation of eye morphology features, facilitating accurate modeling of pupil and iris. Then (b) apply a novel topologically guided modularity-aware graph clustering approach to precisely track the movement of the pupil and address the label sparsity in event-based eye tracking. We show that our unsupervised approach has comparable performance against the supervised approaches while consistently outperforming the conventional clustering approaches.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')

Reviewers are expected to have at least two papers in top peer-reviewed conferences or journals, with at least one paper in a machine learning venue (e.g., NeurIPS, ICML, or ICLR) in the last three years, though we still ask that you nominate one of the authors even if none meet this requirement. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.
